title: Room Booker Without Overlaps
statement:
Build the booking logic for a single meeting room. Each request asks for the time span [start, end): it includes start and excludes end, so a meeting ending at 20 and one starting at 20 do not clash.

  • RoomBooker() creates an empty schedule.
  • book(start, end) accepts the request and returns true if it overlaps no booking accepted so far. Otherwise it returns false and the schedule is unchanged.

Tests are a list of operations and their arguments; the first operation creates the object. The expected output has one entry per operation (null for the constructor).

examples.why: [15, 25) overlaps [10, 20) on 15..19. [20, 30) only touches it at 20, which [10, 20) does not include.
Neither end of [0, 100) falls inside [20, 30), yet it swallows the whole booking. Checking only the endpoints misses this.
The rejected [5, 15) is never stored, so [10, 15) fits.

hints: Two half-open spans [a, b) and [c, d) overlap exactly when a < d and c < b. Checking that against every booking works, but costs O(n) per call.
Accepted bookings never overlap, so if you keep them sorted by start, they are also sorted by end. Which existing bookings could possibly clash with a new one?
Binary-search for where the new start would go. Only the booking just before that spot and the one just after it can overlap. If neither does, insert it there.

explain.intuition:
The overlap test for half-open spans is one line: [a, b) and [c, d) clash when a < d && c < b. It catches partial overlaps and full containment alike, which endpoint-in-range checks miss.

To make it fast, keep accepted bookings sorted. Because they never overlap, they form a clean timeline. A new booking can only collide with its immediate neighbours on that timeline: the last booking that starts before it, and the first that starts at or after it. A binary search finds that spot in O(log n). It is how a calendar UI knows instantly whether a dragged event lands on top of another one.
steps: Keep a list of accepted bookings sorted by start.
For book(start, end), binary-search the first index i whose start is ≥ start.
If booking i exists and its start is < end, it clashes: return false.
If booking i − 1 exists and its end is > start, it clashes: return false.
Otherwise insert the new booking at index i and return true.
pitfalls: Treating the end as included. Then back-to-back meetings like [10, 20) and [20, 30) are wrongly rejected.
Only checking whether the new start or end lies inside an old booking. A new span that covers an old one entirely slips through.
Storing a booking before you know it fits, so a rejected request still blocks later ones.

complexity.time: O(log n) search per call, plus O(n) array insert (O(log n) with a balanced tree)

solutions.title: Compare with every booking
solutions.idea: Keep a plain list and test the new span against each accepted booking.

solutions.title: Sorted timeline with binary search
solutions.idea: Accepted bookings sorted by start are also sorted by end. Only the neighbours of the insertion point can clash.

followups: Allow up to two overlapping bookings at any moment, but never three. What do you need to track?
Return how many bookings overlap at the busiest moment after each call, with no rejections.
